title: The ball that never stops bouncing

data.source: Filippov (1960), Johansson, Egerstedt, Lygeros and Sastry (1999), Goebel, Sanfelice and Teel (2012); cited from memory. Computed and simulated, seeded.

prediction: CRR's cut-and-seed is a well-posed hybrid system with no pile-up of cuts under R4's conditions, by the standard argument; in fact any continuous path makes at most (highest point - start)/a cuts, so the pile-up is ruled out by the fixed cut distance alone; and with noise the cut time is discontinuous only on grazing paths, a vanishing share.
baseline: Hybrid-systems theory: Zeno behaviour (Johansson et al. 1999), well-posedness (Goebel, Sanfelice and Teel 2012), Filippov (1960). Decoy: cuts by time t are at most t over the mean gap.
relation: a special case of the dwell-time argument; R4's condition tau > A is not needed for it
status_line: CRR here is: an assumption the standard result does not need (no pile-up of cuts follows from a fixed cut distance and no blow-up, not from tau > A); otherwise a special case of hybrid-systems theory.
why: R4 (Phoenix status ASSUMPTION) says its no-pile-up conclusion is 'a standard hybrid-ODE argument', and it is: the bounds held on every random system. But the conclusion needs less. Each cut raises the path's high-water mark by a, so any continuous path makes finitely many cuts in finite time, noise or no noise; pile-up needs the path to run off to infinity or the cut distance to shrink. What R4's conditions buy is that every occasion completes, and smooth dependence on the start. With noise, the cut time jumps on paths that graze the threshold, and the share of such paths shrank with the size of the nudge.
